$comment: Exercise workbook source. Exercises 1-3 are collected and marked; Exercise 4 is private to the delegate and never collected.

exercises.title: Name six containers
exercises.brief: You are the mechanical engineer at PLNS on the **Kigali Innovation Hub** (project code `KIH`). The project is not subdivided into zones. Name the six information containers below. Where information is missing, state the assumption you make.

items.ask: Your 3D mechanical model, covering the whole project, all levels. First of its kind.
items.why: All levels is ZZ, not a specific floor. M3 for a model.

items.ask: A ductwork layout drawing for level 03. Twelfth drawing in the series.
items.why: DR for a drawing, level 03 is specific.

items.ask: The architect's (originator code ARCH) general arrangement drawing for the ground floor. Third in series.
items.why: The ORIGINATOR changes to ARCH and the ROLE to A. Tests that delegates separate the two fields.

items.ask: Your mechanical equipment schedule, whole project, all levels. First in series.
A clash report produced by the BIM coordinator at PLNS, covering the whole project. Second in series.
items.why: Role Z - general, non-disciplinary. A clash report is not a mechanical deliverable. This is the hardest item.

items.ask: The structural engineer's (originator STRU) calculations for the level 01 slab. Ninth in series.

exercises.marking: One mark per fully correct name; half a mark for a name with exactly one field wrong. Items 3 and 5 are the discriminators - 3 tests originator-versus-role, 5 tests the non-disciplinary role code.
exercises.teachingNote: Item 5 will produce debate. Let it run for two minutes. The point is that role describes the discipline of the CONTENT, and a federated clash report belongs to no single discipline.

exercises.title: Route eight documents
exercises.brief: For each document below, state (a) which CDE state it belongs in, (b) which code it carries - a suitability code if shared, an authorization code if published - and (c) the revision code. Two of these are deliberately ambiguous: say what you would do and what you would check.

items.ask: A draft mechanical layout the engineer is still working on. Nobody else has seen it.
items.why: Not for issue. Sits in WIP.

items.ask: A structural frame model issued so the MEP team can route services through it. Second preliminary issue.
items.why: Coordination - carries an expectation of use.

items.ask: A topographical survey issued so the whole team is aware of site constraints. Nobody is to design to it yet.
items.why: Information only - no expectation of use.

items.ask: A draft specification sent to the client asking for their comments. First issue.
A general arrangement drawing approved by the client at the end of stage 3, with no comments.
items.why: PUBLISHED CARRIES AN AUTHORIZATION CODE, NOT A SUITABILITY CODE. This is the item that teaches the two code families.

items.ask: The same drawing, approved but with three comments the architect must resolve next revision.
A drawing at P05 that the contractor has started building from, but which the client has not formally approved.
items.why: There is no correct answer. If it is being built from, it should be Published and at C01 - but it has not been authorised, so it cannot be. The honest answer: STOP. This is a live risk, not a filing question. Check the BEP's approval process and escalate. A delegate who says 'it depends' and explains why has answered correctly.

items.ask: A model issued to a sub-consultant who is not named in the project's CDE permissions.
items.why: The state and code are the easy part - the problem is that the recipient is outside the CDE, so the transfer is uncontrolled and unlogged. Check the BEP, and whether ISO 19650-5 security requirements apply. The answer is a process failure, not a code.

exercises.marking: Half a mark for each of state, code and revision on items 1-6 (9 marks). Items 7 and 8 are marked on reasoning only, 1.5 marks each: full marks for recognising the ambiguity and naming what they would check; zero for confidently inventing an answer.
exercises.teachingNote: Items 7 and 8 exist to build the reflex the whole course depends on: when the standard does not settle it, the BEP does - and when the BEP does not settle it either, you escalate rather than guess. Do not let a delegate talk you into a 'right answer' for these.

exercises.title: Draft BEP clauses and a MIDP
exercises.method: Guided drafting, on paper and in the supplied spreadsheet.
exercises.brief: Using the supplied delivery programme, complete three BEP clauses and build a ten-row MIDP.

parts.ask: Draft the BEP clause covering the **naming convention**. It must state the field order, give a worked example, and say where the code tables are defined.
parts.answer: Must contain: the seven-field order; a worked example using the project's own code; and an explicit statement of where the type/role/suitability tables are defined for this project (an appendix, or a named standard). A clause that gives the format but does not say where the code tables live has not settled anything.

parts.ask: Draft the BEP clause covering the **CDE**. It must name the four states, say who may write to each, and describe the approval process for moving into Published.
parts.answer: Must contain: four named states; write permission per state; and a NAMED ROLE authorised to approve into Published. A clause that says 'the project lead approves' without saying who that is, or what happens in their absence, fails the test.

parts.ask: Draft the BEP clause covering the **coordinate system and units**. One paragraph.
parts.answer: Must state: the coordinate system, the project base point, the units (mm), and that these are fixed at mobilisation and never changed. The 'never changed' commitment is the substance of the clause.

parts.ask: Build a ten-row MIDP from the supplied delivery programme. Every row must carry at minimum the deliverable, the responsible party and the date.
parts.answer: One mark per row that carries all three of what/who/when. Award nothing extra for additional columns, but note that a delegate who adds suitability-at-delivery or a TIDP reference is thinking correctly about the document as a control instrument.

exercises.marking: 26 marks. Parts A-C are marked on whether the clause SETTLES the question, not on prose quality. The test for every clause: could two task teams read this and still disagree? If yes, it fails.
exercises.teachingNote: Delegates write vague clauses because vague clauses feel safe. Push back hard on any clause containing 'as appropriate', 'as required' or 'to be agreed'. Those three phrases are how a BEP becomes decorative.

exercises.title: Audit your own project
exercises.method: Private. Not collected, not marked, not seen by the instructor.
exercises.brief: Run the six-point self-audit against a project you are working on right now. Answer honestly - nobody will see this.
exercises.teachingNote: This is the most important fifteen minutes of the day and it must stay private. A person who publicly admits their project is non-compliant gets defensive; a person who discovers it privately gets motivated. Say explicitly, twice, that it will not be collected. Do not walk the room looking over shoulders.
